titleStmt.title: To Harriet Shaw Weaver. Wednesday, 10 November 1920
titleStmt.author: James Joyce

seriesStmt.p: Machine readable texts of the unpublished correspondence of James Joyce

projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

seg.quote: It seems that the case is on its way now to a third hearing and I knew nothing about it till Mr Pound sent me on Mr Quinn's letters.

div.p: Mr Huebsch was here but on me he made anything but a favourable impression. He hinted that if a European edition of the book were printed in Paris he could pirate it in New York. Mr Quinn and Mr Pound wish me to cable to New York withdrawing Ulysses from The Little Review so that further publication may not cause further prosecution, which might have the effect of dissuading Mr Huebsch from bringing out the special edition which Mr Quinn plans. In my opinion, however, Mr Huebsch’s attitude will not be influenced by that so much as by other considerations. Until I have more information on this point I am reluctant to cable as Mr Quinn and Mr Pound suggest because it seems to me that to do so would be to pass sentence on my own writing and to blame the editors of the review for having published it and to prejudice their position at the next hearing of the case without altering the situation favourably. The attitude of Mr Quinn and Mr Pound towards the review is very hostile and there may be other circumstances at present unknown to me, which justify their attitude. On the other hand I believe I am conscious (and have been for some time past) of vacillation in the minds of many admirers of the book: and any indication on my part that such vacillation was grounded would strengthen it to my detriment. Finally the episode which I am writing might have the effect of nullifying the action suggested to me even if I took that course.

seg.quote: Circe has been very much delayed by a number of causes – my journey here, all the unsatisfactory interviews I have had here with people who seemingly do not know their own intentions ...

div.note: For context, see JJ to Pound, 5 November 1920, notes 2, 8 and 10.

In a letter of 15 August 1920 (John Quinn Memorial Collection, Manuscripts & Archives Division, New York Public Library), Quinn had proposed a private American edition, to be published by B. W. Huebsch, limited to 1,000 or 1,250 copies selling for $8 or $10 each. Such an edition, intended for limited distribution to subscribers only, would enable JJ to publish Ulysses without any cuts or alterations to the manuscript and might escape prosecution on obscenity charges.
